title: DevOps Engineer Salary in 2026: US Pay Guide
metaDescription: DevOps engineer salaries in the US for 2026 — average pay by experience level, the highest-paying employers and cities, and the skills that raise pay.
headline: DevOps Engineer Salary in the US: 2026 Guide

sections.title: Average DevOps Engineer Salary in the US for 2026
sections.content:
DevOps engineers remain among the better-paid roles in software, with 2026 postings on Indeed averaging around $132,500 to $133,350. Jobicy's October 2026 data puts the national average slightly lower at $128,000, reflecting a broad mix of junior through senior roles. The gap between the two figures mostly comes down to how each source samples postings, but both point to a market comfortably above six figures.

That average hides a wide spread. Salary.com's September 2026 numbers show entry-level DevOps roles around $82,000, mid-career engineers near $134,000 and senior engineers around $150,000. In practice, company size, industry and location move the needle as much as the title itself — the same engineer can be worth dramatically different amounts in different markets.

sections.title: DevOps Pay by Experience Level
sections.content:
Experience is the single biggest driver of DevOps pay. Jobicy's October 2026 breakdown puts junior engineers with 0 to 2 years of experience at $76,300 to $105,100, mid-level engineers with 3 to 5 years at $104,400 to $157,100, and senior engineers with 6 or more years at $157,800 to $242,200. Clearing the six-year mark roughly doubles the junior range.

The jump from mid to senior is where the money concentrates, because senior engineers own reliability decisions, architecture trade-offs and incident leadership that directly protect revenue. If you are early in your career, the fastest path upward is shipping production systems with real uptime responsibility rather than collecting tools on a resume.

sections.title: Highest-Paying Employers and Cities
sections.content:
A small set of employers pay far above the market. Siemens leads Jobicy's October 2026 employer list at roughly $301,600, followed by Grammarly at about $267,000 and Dow Jones near $265,000. These tend to be large enterprises or well-funded product companies where DevOps work sits close to revenue-critical systems.

Location matters almost as much as employer. Annapolis Junction, Maryland tops the city list at roughly $176,000 to $178,000 — a defense and government contracting hub — followed by Washington DC at $142,000 to $143,000, New York at $139,000 to $141,000, Chicago near $137,700 and Dallas at $136,000 to $137,000. In San Francisco, lead DevOps roles reach a median near $228,000.

sections.title: Skills and Certifications That Raise Pay
sections.content:
The tools that command the biggest premiums are the ones behind modern cloud platforms: Kubernetes, Terraform and AWS dominate job requirements. Engineers who can design infrastructure as code, build reliable CI/CD pipelines and operate production clusters are consistently the hardest to hire, which is why those skills translate directly into higher offers.

Certifications help most when they validate skills you already use. The AWS Certified DevOps Engineer – Professional, the Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) and the Terraform Associate are the three credentials employers mention most often. Broader hybrid roles also pay well: platform-engineer and MLOps-hybrid positions earn roughly 20% above standard DevOps roles because they combine operations expertise with scarce specialist skills.

sections.title: How Competitive Is the DevOps Market in 2026?
sections.content:
DevOps is a competitive field to break into. Market data puts the supply-to-demand ratio near 1.9 to 1, meaning nearly two engineers compete for every open role — demand is strong, but so is the pipeline of candidates. Underlying demand is driven by ongoing cloud migration and the industry's reliance on CI/CD pipelines to ship software faster and more safely.

The practical takeaway is that junior engineers need differentiation. A public portfolio of real infrastructure work, contributions to open-source tooling, and hands-on experience with the core stack — Kubernetes, Terraform, AWS — moves applications to the top of the pile far more reliably than applying at volume.
